There's an impressive lack of self-awareness on this campus. I never thought I’d say this, but it seems like the Stud’s TeaDo is brewing more than just tea—it’s steeping a campus-wide obsession. Let me tell you, the buzz isn’t just about the caffeine. I’ve been seeing the same faces in line at TeaDo every day, and it’s not just coincidence. We’re talking about a full-fledged boba addict battalion, and I’m right there with them.

It’s got to the point where even my therapist is raising eyebrows, saying they’re seeing a wave of students coming in at MIT Medical, all with bubble tea obsessions.

I will say, it is a weird kind of solidarity, knowing you're not the only one hooked on the tapioca train to bliss town. There's a certain camaraderie now, a silent nod we give each other in TeaDo. It’s as if we’re all part of this secret society where the handshake is replaced with the clink of ice in a plastic cup. We don’t have to say a word—our eyes say enough... 'Yeah, I’m getting my daily fix too.'

We’re all juggling p-sets, friends, and boba, and the shared dependence on that sweet, chewy goodness honestly got me weirdly feeling connected to strangers mid-semester. It’s a collective addiction, one that’s as comforting as it is concerning.

So, here’s to my fellow boba aficionados, my comrades in arms. We might be in too deep, but at least we’re in it together uwu. TeaDo has unwittingly become the watering hole for a new kind of MIT student—the boba-holic. And while our GPAs might not thank us, our taste buds sure as heck do, heck yeaaa :3

1. Filter out our dorm spam
2. Don’t walk in the Infinite
3. Avoid lunch at dining halls
4. Get a good TV and make your dorm cozy (Big Joe or a small freezer)

The other day, I walked past a grad student (or prof?) with their child in the Infinite. They said to their child something like, '...you should probably get out of the way [of the students] since they’re all doing serious things and you don’t want to waste their time... I mean, you're in third grade, so it's probably different for you, but they are doing serious things...' And it made me realize how unserious MIT really is. Sure, there are serious things—burnout, pressure, social isolation—but I actually like most of my lectures and problem sets, and I like being close to my friends. Being here feels less serious than my time in third grade. I think I might have truly found paradise here.
